beginner_glossary.ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Ci: A chip custom-designed for ONE specific job (e.g., a particular company's AI accelerator), as opposed to a flexible, off-the-shelf chip like an NVIDIA GPU. Alchip helps companies design and manufacture their own ASICs.
beginner_glossary.Custom silicon / XPU: A hyperscaler's own AI accelerator chip (Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium, etc.). Big cloud companies build these to cut cost and reduce dependence on NVIDIA. 'XPU' is a generic term for such custom accelerators. Alchip is one of the firms that turns these designs into real, manufacturable chips.
beginner_glossary.ASIC design service house: A company that provides the engineering to take a chip from concept/architecture to a finished, manufacturable product — physical design, integration, and managing manufacturing/packaging/test. Alchip, Broadcom, Marvell, and GUC are examples. Alchip is a PURE design-service house (it sells no chips or IP of its own).
beginner_glossary.NRE (Non-Recurring Engineering): The one-time design fees a customer pays Alchip to engineer a chip BEFORE any volume production. NRE is high-margin and front-loaded; it was 'very strong' in Q1 2026 and is what kept margins high while production revenue was low.
beginner_glossary.Production revenue (vs NRE): Once a chip is designed, Alchip also earns money making/shipping it in volume (it buys wafers from TSMC, has them packaged/tested, and sells finished chips to the customer). Production revenue is larger but lower-margin than NRE. The 2026 story is production revenue ramping as the N3 accelerator ships.
beginner_glossary.COT (Customer-Owned Tooling): A business model where the customer owns the chip design/IP and hires Alchip mainly to implement and manufacture it. As volumes get huge, hyperscalers increasingly prefer COT — which Alchip says favors a neutral service house like itself.
beginner_glossary.PD0 / PD1 / PD2: Levels of how much design work Alchip does. Higher PD levels (PD1/PD2) mean Alchip adds more design value (higher margin); 'production-only' work adds the least value and lowest margin. Alchip is cautious about taking production-only jobs.
beginner_glossary.Physical design / back-end integration: The engineering that turns a chip's logical design into the actual transistor-level layout that can be manufactured, then stitches all the pieces (compute die, I/O die, memory) into one working chip. This is Alchip's core expertise; it says it is the ONLY physical-design vendor for its N3 and N2 accelerator projects.
beginner_glossary.Process node (N3 / N2 / N5 / N7): TSMC's chip-manufacturing generations ('N3' = 3-nanometer-class, 'N2' = 2nm). Smaller numbers = newer, faster, denser, more expensive. Alchip works at the leading edge: N3/N2/N5/N7 were >80% of its Q1 2026 revenue. The shift from N3 to N2 roughly doubles the value Alchip captures per project.
beginner_glossary.Tape-out: The moment a chip design is finalized and sent to the foundry (TSMC) to be manufactured. Alchip plans to 'tape out' its N2 accelerator by end of 2026, with production revenue ~2028.
beginner_glossary.HPC (High-Performance Computing): Data-center computing for AI and heavy workloads. HPC was 70% of Alchip's Q1 2026 revenue — i.e., AI accelerators are its main business.
beginner_glossary.Chiplet: Instead of one big chip, a design split into several smaller 'tiles' (compute die, I/O die, etc.) packaged together. The N2 accelerator is a chiplet design, which raises both complexity and the price/value Alchip captures.
beginner_glossary.CoWoS / advanced packaging: TSMC's flagship method of combining the processor with stacks of HBM memory into one large AI package. Alchip secures CoWoS capacity for its customers; it says wafers (not CoWoS) are currently the bottleneck.
beginner_glossary.HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory): Stacked DRAM placed next to an AI chip for fast data access. In Alchip's projects the HBM is 'consigned' (supplied by the customer), not bought by Alchip.
beginner_glossary.Wafer / wafer capacity / turnaround time: A wafer is the silicon disk on which chips are made. 'N3 capacity is the most precious thing in the industry' — getting enough leading-edge wafers from TSMC limits how much Alchip can ship. The full turnaround (wafer + CoWoS) is ~6–7 months, which caps near-term upside.
beginner_glossary.Gross margin: Percent of revenue left after the direct cost of the work. Alchip's was a high 50% in Q1 2026 because of the NRE-heavy mix; management expects it to TREND DOWN later in 2026 as lower-margin production revenue grows (even though total profit rises).
beginner_glossary.EPS (Earnings Per Share): Net profit per share. Q1 2026 EPS was NT$17.55; FY2025 was NT$69.2; trailing-twelve-month was NT$67.05 (2026-06-13).
beginner_glossary.P/E ratio / Forward P/E: Share price divided by earnings per share. Alchip's TRAILING P/E was ~61x (on depressed 2025/early-2026 earnings) but FORWARD P/E only ~24x (2026-06-13) — the gap reflects how much earnings are expected to recover as the N3 ramp hits.

company_snapshot.what_it_is: Alchip is a Taiwan-listed (Cayman-incorporated) PURE-PLAY ASIC design-service company. It does NOT sell its own chips or IP; instead it engineers and manufactures CUSTOM silicon for other companies — most importantly, the AI accelerators (custom 'XPUs') that hyperscalers build to rival NVIDIA's GPUs. In the AI/semiconductor supply chain it sits in the chip-design/component layer: it takes a customer's accelerator design, does the physical design and integration on TSMC's leading-edge nodes (N3, N2), secures wafer + CoWoS + substrate + test capacity, and ships finished chips. Its self-described edge is NEUTRALITY — because it makes no competing products, every IP and packaging partner is willing to work with it.
company_snapshot.headquarters: Taipei / Hsinchu, Taiwan (with design centers in Japan, Malaysia, Vietnam, and the U.S.)
company_snapshot.founder_ceo: Chairman & CEO: Johnny Shen. CFO: Daniel Wang. Recently hired a Chief Business Officer ('Freddy', ex-NVIDIA / Xilinx) to deepen U.S. hyperscaler relationships.
company_snapshot.manufacturing_footprint: Fabless — Alchip designs chips and outsources manufacturing to TSMC (wafers + CoWoS packaging). It is deliberately diversifying its ENGINEERING resources outside China (Japan office up to 250 staff; Malaysia + Vietnam 120+ engineers combined) to manage geopolitical risk; China work is focused on automotive/robotics/consumer at N3 and above. [Q1 2026 call 2026-05-27]
end_markets: AI / HPC accelerators (custom XPUs for hyperscalers) — the core

business_model.summary: Alchip earns money in two linked phases. First, NRE (non-recurring engineering): high-margin, front-loaded design fees a customer pays to have Alchip engineer a chip. Second, PRODUCTION: once the chip is designed, Alchip buys the wafers from TSMC, manages packaging/test, and sells finished chips in volume — larger revenue but lower margin. The whole company is a leveraged bet on the rise of CUSTOM AI silicon: as hyperscalers build their own accelerators to cut cost and reduce NVIDIA dependence, they need a neutral, leading-edge design-service partner — which is exactly what Alchip is. Revenue is lumpy because it swings between NRE-heavy (design) and production-heavy phases per chip generation.
how_they_make_money: NRE design fees (high margin, front-loaded): engineering custom accelerators, CPUs, and networking ASICs — 'very strong', especially from North American hyperscalers. [Q1 2026 call]

Production / volume chip sales (larger, lower margin): shipping finished chips (e.g., the N3 AI accelerator ramping from June 2026), where Alchip sources TSMC wafers + CoWoS + substrate + test. [Q1 2026 call]
By application (Q1 2026): HPC/AI accelerators 70% of revenue; plus automotive (China), networking ASICs, and selective Arm server CPUs. [Q1 2026 call]
competitive_moat_analyst_view: Neutrality: Alchip sells no chips or IP of its own, so it has no conflict of interest with customers — every IP/packaging/optical partner (e.g., Ayar Labs, NVLink ecosystem) will work with it. Management calls this its core differentiator vs. product-making rivals. [Q1 2026 call]
Leading-edge physical-design expertise: it claims to be the ONLY physical-design vendor on its N3 and N2 accelerator projects, and a leader in number of tape-outs/design wins.
TSMC relationship + capacity access: tight cooperation with TSMC for scarce N3 wafers and CoWoS — a real advantage when wafers are the bottleneck.
Anchor accelerator customer: one dominant hyperscaler accelerator account (see customer concentration risk) that is 'one of the most important accounts in the industry'.

ASSUMPTION-flavored: the moat is real in pure-play ASIC service, but Broadcom and Marvell are far larger and also enable custom silicon; Alchip's edge is being the focused, neutral specialist rather than the biggest.

revenue_streams.analyst_view: Alchip is essentially a leveraged play on ONE thing: the ramp of custom AI accelerators on TSMC's leading edge. Q1 2026 was an intentional air-pocket — production was low and NRE was high, which flattered margins (50%) but cut revenue 58% YoY. The whole investment case is the back-end-loaded recovery: N3 accelerator production from June 2026 → much stronger Q3/Q4 → full-year revenue expected to surpass the 2024 peak → then the higher-value N2 generation in 2028. Automotive and networking add diversification, but the accelerator ramp (and its single dominant customer) is what moves the stock.

competitors.landscape_summary: Alchip competes in custom-silicon (ASIC) design services for AI/HPC. The field is small — management says 'maybe 5 fingers' of real competitors — dominated by two much larger players (Broadcom and Marvell) plus other Taiwan design houses (GUC, MediaTek). Alchip's positioning is the focused, NEUTRAL pure-play (no own products/IP), competing on engineering quality, leading-edge node expertise, tape-out track record, and TSMC capacity access rather than scale.

competitors.differentiation_analyst_view: Alchip's pitch is 'pure-play + neutral + leading-edge'. Because it sells no competing products, it avoids the conflicts that product-makers (Broadcom, Marvell, MediaTek) carry, and partners across the IP/optical/interconnect ecosystem will work with it. Its real disadvantages are SCALE and CUSTOMER RELATIONSHIPS — rivals are far bigger and more entrenched at the top of hyperscaler org charts (hence the ex-NVIDIA CBO hire). The competitive reality: more designs are up for grabs as hyperscalers dual-source, so Alchip can win meaningful share without 'winning all', but it is the small player in a field of giants.

financial_performance.analyst_view: Alchip's financials tell a clean 'trough-to-recovery' story. 2025 revenue fell ~39% because the lead customer skipped a generation, yet net income only fell ~11% as the mix went NRE-heavy (Q1 2026 gross margin hit 50%). Now production is set to re-accelerate hard from June 2026, so revenue should rebound sharply (management says above the 2024 peak) while margins normalize lower. The model's weakness is LUMPINESS and single-customer dependence; its strength is very high incremental profitability on design work and visibility through 2029 on secured N3/N2 programs.

valuation.analyst_view: This is a high-beta, small-cap (~US$10.5B) leveraged play on custom AI silicon — very different from a megacap. The bull view: forward P/E ~24x is reasonable for a company about to grow revenue past its prior peak with visibility to 2029. The bear view: the multiple still assumes a flawless N3 ramp and continued reliance on essentially ONE dominant accelerator customer, in a small, volatile name where any slip (yield, wafer allocation, a lost generation like 2025) can hit the stock hard. The debate is less about whether AI-ASIC demand is real (it clearly is) and more about execution risk and customer concentration at a still-rich forward multiple.

risks.why_it_matters: Alchip openly states it has only ONE major hyperscaler accelerator account today; losing it, or that customer skipping a generation (as happened in 2025), would severely hit revenue.

risks.risk: Execution / yield on the N3 ramp
risks.why_it_matters: The 2026 thesis depends on the N3 accelerator ramping on time at good yield; any production or yield stumble directly cuts the expected recovery.
Upside is capped by how many scarce N3 wafers TSMC can supply (~6–7 month turnaround); capacity shortfalls limit shipments even when demand is strong.
Revenue and margins swing sharply between design-heavy and production-heavy phases per generation, making results volatile and hard to model.
Broadcom and Marvell are far bigger custom-silicon enablers; GUC, MediaTek, and Qualcomm also compete — pressuring win rates and pricing.
Hyperscalers may build more design capability in-house or split projects across vendors, limiting Alchip's share per design.

Automotive work is China-centric and engineering had been China-heavy; export controls or cross-strait tension could disrupt customers, talent, or supply (mitigated by diversifying engineering to Japan/Malaysia/Vietnam).
Even on forward earnings (~24x) the stock prices in a strong recovery; with a 52-week range of NT$2,480–5,640, disappointment can cause large drawdowns.
Demand depends on hyperscaler AI capex; a broad AI-spending digestion would slow accelerator programs and Alchip's ramp.
Gross margin falls as lower-margin production revenue grows; if pricing pressure exceeds plan, profit growth could lag revenue growth.

final_research_summary.one_paragraph: Alchip Technologies (3661.TW) is a Taiwan-listed, Cayman-incorporated PURE-PLAY ASIC design-service house — it engineers and manufactures the custom AI accelerators ('XPUs') that hyperscalers build to rival NVIDIA's GPUs, doing the leading-edge physical design and managing TSMC wafers + CoWoS + test. Its self-described edge is NEUTRALITY: it sells no chips or IP of its own, so the whole IP/optical/interconnect ecosystem will partner with it. The financial story is a clean trough-to-recovery: FY2025 (reported 2026-03-18) revenue fell ~39% to US$992M because the top customer skipped a product generation, yet net income held up far better (US$179.4M, EPS NT$69.2) thanks to a high-margin NRE mix; Q1 2026 (reported 2026-05-27) was the deliberate trough — revenue US$132.4M (-58.5% YoY) but a 50% gross margin and US$45.1M net income (EPS NT$17.55), with HPC 70% of sales. The inflection is now: the #1 customer's N3 AI accelerator began shipping ~June 2026 and ramps hard, so management guides a back-end-loaded year with full-year revenue expected to SURPASS the 2024 peak (~US$1.6B), the higher-value N2 chiplet generation taping out by end-2026 for ~2028 production, and visibility through 2029. On valuation, the stock (~NT$4,105, ~NT$335B / ~US$10.5B market cap, 52-week range NT$2,480–5,640) looks extreme on trailing earnings (~61x P/E at the trough) but reasonable on forward earnings (~24x), so it is priced as a recovery/growth story; consensus is 'Buy' (~23 analysts, avg target ~NT$5,733). What is FACT is a real, profitable, leading-edge custom-silicon franchise with secured N3/N2 programs; what is being PRICED is a flawless N3 ramp and continued reliance on essentially ONE dominant accelerator customer — so the core risks are execution and customer concentration, not whether the AI-ASIC wave is real.
